questions.question_text:
A ball is thrown from the origin at $12\text{ m/s}$ at $60^{\circ}$ above the horizontal.
Take $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$.
Which is $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$?

options.why: Applied gravity to the horizontal component as well, but $\ddot{x}=0$.
Swapped sine and cosine when resolving the initial speed.
Both slips: components swapped and gravity applied to the horizontal component.

questions.question_text:
A projectile launched from the origin has $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)=7\underset{\sim}{i}+(26-9.8t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ metres per second.
Which is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$?

options.why: Integrated $-9.8t$ as $-9.8t^{2}$, forgetting to halve the coefficient.
Left the constant horizontal velocity un-integrated, so $x$ does not grow with time.
Both slips: the horizontal term not integrated and the $t^{2}$ coefficient not halved.

questions.question_text:
A stone is thrown from the top of a cliff $16\text{ m}$ above the sea, with $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)=13\underset{\sim}{i}+(22-10t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ metres per second and $y$ measured from sea level.
Which is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$?

options.why: Assumed launch from ground level, dropping the $16\text{ m}$ height of the cliff.
Put the launch height into the horizontal component instead of the vertical one.
Added the launch height to both components, although the stone starts at $x=0$.

questions.question_text:
A particle is projected from the origin with initial velocity $\underset{\sim}{v}(0)=16\underset{\sim}{i}+23\underset{\sim}{j}$ metres per second.
Take $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$.
Which is $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$?

options.why: Applied gravity to both components instead of only the vertical component.
Used positive vertical acceleration although gravity acts downwards.
Integrated the vertical acceleration twice when finding velocity.

questions.question_text:
A particle is projected from the origin at $10\text{ m/s}$ at $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)$ above the horizontal.
Take $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$.
Which pair gives $x$ and $y$?

options.why: Swapped sine and cosine when resolving the initial speed.
Integrated $-10t$ as $-10t^{2}$ instead of $-5t^{2}$.
Both slips: components swapped and the $t^{2}$ coefficient not halved.

questions.question_text:
A ball is thrown from the origin at $20\text{ m/s}$ at $30^{\circ}$ **below** the horizontal.
Take $g=9.8\text{ m/s}^{2}$.
Which is $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$?

options.why: Treated the launch as above the horizontal, giving a positive initial vertical velocity.
Swapped sine and cosine when resolving the initial speed.
Both slips: components swapped and the downward launch treated as upward.

questions.question_text:
A ball launched from a platform has $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=21t\underset{\sim}{i}+(28t-4.9t^{2}+5)\underset{\sim}{j}$ metres, with $y$ measured from the ground.
What is the launch speed?

options.why: Added the initial component sizes $21+28$ instead of using Pythagoras.
Used only the initial vertical component and ignored the horizontal component.
Used only the initial horizontal component and ignored the vertical component.
